title: Sexual violence in perspective
text:
Worldwide sexual-assault comparisons often begin with a country ranking. A more useful starting point is the question behind the number: are we looking at people’s experiences, offences recorded by police, or cases reaching a justice outcome?
These sources reveal different parts of a serious problem. They should be read together without being treated as interchangeable.
This article presents the main findings from my full report, Sexual violence in perspective, with adult and older-adolescent evidence separated from childhood experiences. The full version includes searchable country tables, downloadable data and detailed source notes. Evidence was checked on 6 November 2026.

title: Sexual violence in perspective
section: A worldwide comparison with a defined scope
text:
A worldwide comparison with a defined scope
WHO’s 2023 estimates draw on studies and surveys conducted between 2000 and 2023. Its harmonised non-partner sexual-violence measure concerns women aged 15 and over who experienced violence since age 15. It excludes a current or former intimate partner, and includes older adolescents within its age band.
The downloaded portal snapshot contains estimates for 138 countries and areas. The UK estimate is 7.3%, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 4.6%–11.0%. This is an estimate labelled United Kingdom, rather than an England and Wales survey statistic. WHO data and definitions.

Figure 1. Selected WHO 2023 estimates, presented alphabetically. The UK is highlighted; lines show 95% uncertainty intervals. Source: WHO VAW portal, accessed 6 November 2026.
These are lifetime experiences since age 15, not annual rates. A recent estimation year also does not mean every country supplied a recent survey. WHO’s UK inputs in the portal include surveys from 2007 and 2012.
A further distinction matters: the familiar WHO headline of around one in three women combines physical and/or sexual partner violence and non-partner sexual violence. It is not a sexual-assault-only rate. WHO global release.

title: Sexual violence in perspective
section: England and Wales now has a redesigned measure
text:
England and Wales now has a redesigned measure
The Crime Survey for England and Wales estimates that 2.1% of people aged 16 and over, around one million people, experienced sexual victimisation including attempts in the year ending March 2026. The estimates are 2.8% for women and 1.4% for men.
This redesigned measure includes rape or penetration, being forced to penetrate, unwanted touching, exposure and image-related experiences. ONS states that it is not comparable with previously published measures. ONS latest crime bulletin.

Figure 2. A new sexual-victimisation series, including experiences beyond contact assault. Source: ONS; CSEW year ending March 2026. Do not calculate a change from the former measure.

title: Sexual violence in perspective
section: The earlier trend has its own boundary
text:
The earlier trend has its own boundary
The former sexual-assault measure can be followed using a consistent age range of 16–59. Its 2025 estimate was 2.4%, significantly higher than 1.7% in 2015. The change from 2.6% in 2024 was not statistically significant. ONS prevalence and trends.

Figure 3. Last-year sexual assault including attempts, England and Wales. Source: ONS. No estimate for 2021; source quality cautions apply in 2022–2025. The 2026 redesign is not joined to this line.
The detailed 2025 release also shows higher prevalence among younger people. It uses the earlier definition and cannot be treated as a breakdown of the redesigned 2026 figure. Age, sex and disability patterns in the full report describe associations, not causes.

title: Sexual violence in perspective
section: Childhood experiences need a separate account
text:
Childhood experiences need a separate account
UNICEF estimates that more than 370 million girls and women alive in 2024, around one in eight, experienced rape or sexual assault before age 18. Its corresponding estimate for boys and men is 240–310 million, around one in eleven. These totals include adults recalling childhood; they are not annual counts among today’s children. UNICEF global estimates.

Figure 4. Regional childhood-experience estimates among girls and women, UNICEF 2024. These are lifetime experiences, not annual rates among current children. Underlying coverage varies.
In England and Wales, the redesigned childhood survey estimates that 9.1% of adults aged 18 and over, around 4.3 million people, experienced sexual abuse before age 18. The estimates are 13.9% for women and 4.1% for men. This broader category includes non-contact abuse. ONS childhood bulletin.

Figure 5. Retrospective childhood sexual abuse among adults, CSEW year ending March 2024. Source: ONS. The newer population and pre-18 questions prevent comparison with the former pre-16 series.
The UNICEF and ONS headlines have different definitions and populations. Dividing one by the other would not establish how the UK ranks. Their age bands also overlap the adult-oriented sources, so the figures must not be added together.
England’s children’s services recorded 29,560 children assessed as affected by sexual abuse and 12,120 assessed as affected by exploitation in the year ending March 2025. These can overlap, and service identification is not national prevalence. Department for Education.

title: Sexual violence in perspective
section: Justice figures change as investigations conclude
text:
Justice figures change as investigations conclude
The Home Office initially reported charge/summons outcomes for 3.4% of rape offences recorded in the year ending March 2026. For the previous year’s recording cohort, the rate rose from 2.8% at first release to 5.2% in the later update as more investigations concluded. Home Office outcomes.

Figure 6. England and Wales rape outcomes. The 2025 figures describe the same recording cohort at two snapshots. A charge is not a conviction; the updated figure is not necessarily final. Source: Home Office, section 2.4.
Comparing an updated cohort with a newly recorded one gives cases unequal time to reach an outcome. Dividing convictions in one year by survey-estimated survivors in that year would introduce further mismatches in unit and timing.

title: Sexual violence in perspective
text:
What makes a useful comparison?
A defensible comparison names the population, geography, period and definition. It keeps surveys separate from police records and recognises that more recorded offences can reflect changes in disclosure and recording as well as victimisation.
The full report also explores UNODC recorded-offence rates and the separate systems of England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. It treats missing returns as missing, rather than zero, and presents uncertainty where supplied.
Explore the complete report and sources.
Independent analysis by Kathryn Hopkins. This article discusses sexual violence without graphic descriptions. NHS support information is available for readers who want it.

title: Reporting and the justice response
text:
Population surveys ask about experiences whether or not they were reported. Police data describe incidents brought to official attention and recorded within the relevant rules. The former can reveal hidden victimisation; the latter is important for understanding investigative demand. One cannot substitute for the other.
Changes in law, recording practices and disclosure influence police trends. The ONS 2025 detailed release notes that two offences introduced by the Online Safety Act account for over half the increase in the broad sexual-offence count that year. A change in the broad category is not automatically a change in contact assault. ONS prevalence and trends.
For a subset of reporting forces, 20% of sexual offences recorded in YE March 2025 related to incidents more than 12 months earlier. This is a selected-force statistic, not a complete UK figure, and illustrates why recording year differs from occurrence year.

title: Reporting and the justice response
section: An early charge rate is not final
text:
An early charge rate is not final
The Home Office reports that 3.4% of rape offences recorded in YE March 2026 had a charge/summons outcome in its first annual release. It expects this proportion to rise as investigations conclude. The previous year’s cohort demonstrates why: its rate rose from 2.8% when first published to 5.2% in the later update. Home Office 2025–2026 outcomes, section 2.4.



The initial and subsequently updated charge/summons rate for the 2025 recorded rape cohort, compared with the initial rate for 2026.


The later 2025 figure is still a snapshot, not a guaranteed final outcome. Comparing the updated 2025 rate directly with the first-release 2026 rate would give investigations different follow-up times. A charge/summons outcome is also distinct from prosecution, conviction and sentence.
For rape offences receiving charge/summons outcomes, the source reports a median 438 days from recording to outcome. This is conditional on that outcome group: it is not a waiting time for every survivor or every investigation. Across sexual offences, 26.3% remained without an assigned outcome at year end. Home Office outcomes.
Download the outcome-maturity figures.

title: Reporting and the justice response
section: Why there is no single conviction funnel here
text:
Why there is no single conviction funnel here
An experience measured in a household survey, an offence recorded by police and a defendant convicted by a court are different units. They also occur in different periods. Dividing convictions in a year by survey-estimated victims or offences recorded in that same year does not measure the chance of an assault ending in conviction.
A defensible progression analysis needs linked cohorts, consistent offence scope and sufficient follow-up. This edition does not have those linked records, so it does not invent a population-to-conviction percentage.

title: Reporting and the justice response
text:
Reading relationship statistics carefully
The 2025 ONS release gives victim–perpetrator relationships from 24 police forces. Among female rape victims with a recorded relationship, an intimate partner was the most common category, at 48%. Among male rape victims, acquaintance and other family relative were prominent categories. These are selected police records, not a survey of all survivors and not a description of every UK offence. ONS victim characteristics.
They underline an important boundary of the international chapter: WHO’s non-partner comparison excludes intimate-partner sexual violence and cannot describe the whole burden of sexual assault.

title: The UK in detail
text:
The historical sexual-assault series
To examine the former measure over time, use a consistent 16–59 age band. The 2025 estimate is 2.4%, compared with 1.7% in 2015. ONS identifies that decade difference as statistically significant; the change from 2.6% in 2024 is not significant. These are last-year experiences, not lifetime prevalence. ONS prevalence and trends.



Sexual assault including attempts in the last year among people aged 16–59, ending in 2025 with a gap for 2021.


Survey suspension leaves no 2021 estimate. The source cautions about reduced data collection or sample quality in 2022 and 2023 and half samples in 2024 and 2025. The chart shows point estimates, not confidence bands; it supports only the significance statements made in the source.

title: The UK in detail
text:
Which groups reported higher prevalence?
The detailed 2025 release uses the former sexual-assault measure. Its all-age estimate is 1.9% among people aged 16+; it differs from the 2.4% trend value because the age denominators differ. These 2025 breakdowns should not be treated as breakdowns of the redesigned 2026 estimate.



Sexual-assault prevalence by age in England and Wales, year ending March 2025.


Reported prevalence was higher among people aged 16–34 than among older groups. Full-time students also reported higher prevalence than other occupational groups; ONS notes that this is likely to be linked partly to age. This is a descriptive association, not proof that being a student causes victimisation. ONS victim characteristics.
The same release reports greater prevalence among disabled people than non-disabled people. It does not establish the direction of causation. For regional comparisons, survey differences were not statistically significant; police-recorded regional differences can also reflect reporting and recording practices. Individual risk cannot be inferred from a regional average.

title: Sexual violence in perspective
text:
What the evidence shows
The international comparison is narrower than “all sexual assault”. WHO’s harmonised non-partner measure estimates UK lifetime prevalence at 7.3%, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 4.6%–11.0%, among women aged 15 and over. It excludes violence by a current or former intimate partner. The portal labels the territory United Kingdom; this should not be confused with the England and Wales crime survey. Explore the worldwide comparison.
The latest England and Wales adult survey starts a new series. The redesigned sexual-victimisation questions produce an estimate of around one million people affected in the last year. The measure includes experiences beyond contact assault and cannot be joined to the former sexual-assault trend. Read the UK detail.
Childhood experiences need their own account. UNICEF’s estimates concern experiences before age 18 among people alive at estimation. ONS asks adults to recall their childhood. Neither is an annual estimate of abuse among today’s children. Read the childhood chapter.
Recorded offences and justice outcomes reveal institutional demand and response. They cannot establish how common sexual violence is in the whole population. A charge is not a conviction, and an early charge rate changes as investigations conclude. Read the justice chapter.

How to read “UK”. England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate statistical systems and legal contexts. This report names the jurisdiction on every UK figure. It does not relabel England and Wales as the whole United Kingdom.

title: Worldwide evidence
section: Partner violence is a separate measurement problem
text:
Partner violence is a separate measurement problem
The often-cited WHO global headline of around one in three women combines physical and/or sexual intimate-partner violence and non-partner sexual violence. It is not an estimate that one in three women has been sexually assaulted. A physical-or-sexual indicator cannot isolate sexual violence by itself. WHO global release.
The harmonised country comparison above intentionally uses the sexual-violence-specific non-partner indicator. The report does not add it to physical-or-sexual partner violence: populations and denominators differ, and experiences can overlap.

title: Worldwide evidence
text:
What police-recorded international rates measure
UNODC’s Crime Trends Survey workbook contains national returns for recorded violent and sexual offences. We extract offence rates per 100,000 population, total sex and total age, for rape, sexual assault and the broader sexual-violence category. These remain administrative records. UNODC data and workbook.



Recorded rape offences per 100,000 population in selected jurisdictions in 2022. Countries are alphabetical, with the UK jurisdictions separate.


The common-year illustration uses 2022 because the England and Wales return for these categories stops there in this workbook. Scotland and Northern Ireland have later returns, while some other countries reach 2024. Selecting each country’s latest year would mix periods. All available years remain accessible below.
Higher recorded rates can reflect a combination of higher victimisation, broader definitions, greater willingness to report and more complete recording. Lower recorded rates cannot establish greater safety. The number counts offences rather than unique survivors; recording dates need not be incident dates.

Recorded-offence explorer
The controls initially show rape in 2022. Change year or category to inspect other returns. A missing row is unavailable data, not zero. Do not sum broad sexual violence with its rape and sexual-assault subcategories.

title: Sexual violence during childhood
text:
UNICEF estimates that more than 370 million girls and women alive in 2024, approximately one in eight, experienced rape or sexual assault before age 18. For boys and men, the estimate is 240–310 million, approximately one in eleven. These totals include adults recalling childhood and children already affected. They are not the number of children assaulted in one year. UNICEF global release.



UNICEF regional prevalence estimates of rape or sexual assault before age 18 among girls and women.


The most extensive underlying coverage concerns contact sexual violence against girls and women, using surveys from 2010–2022 in 120 countries and areas. Estimates for boys and men and for non-contact violence use a broader evidence base and some indirect methods. Their precision should not be assumed identical.
When non-contact forms are included, UNICEF’s global totals rise to 650 million girls and women and 410–530 million boys and men. These are broader, overlapping totals; do not add them to the contact figures. Regional rates shown above are point estimates, with no uncertainty intervals provided in this extracted release.

section: England and Wales: adults looking back
text:
England and Wales: adults looking back
The redesigned CSEW childhood questions estimate that 9.1% of adults aged 18 and over, around 4.3 million people, experienced sexual abuse before age 18. The figures are 13.9% for women and 4.1% for men. The sexual-abuse measure includes non-contact abuse, contact abuse, and rape or assault by penetration including attempts. ONS childhood bulletin, YE March 2024.



ONS estimates of sexual abuse experienced before age 18, among adults living in England and Wales at the time of the survey.


These are experiences across many past years, reported by the adult household population at interview. They do not directly measure abuse among children living in England and Wales today, or establish that all recalled abuse occurred within that territory. The newer pre-18 questions and covered population also prevent a trend comparison with the former pre-16 statistics.
Most victims knew a perpetrator. Respondents could report multiple perpetrators and overlapping categories. The fact that 69.8% reported an adult perpetrator and 40.1% an under-18 perpetrator does not imply a total above 100% is an error: some experienced both.

title: Sexual violence during childhood
text:
England: what children’s services identify
The Department for Education records 29,560 children assessed as affected by sexual abuse and 12,120 assessed as affected by sexual exploitation in the year ending 31 March 2025. It also reports 2,190 children starting a child protection plan with sexual abuse as the initial category. DfE statistical release.
These are different service measures. Sexual abuse and exploitation can overlap, and not every child assessed as affected enters a protection plan with that primary category. Counts cannot be added or arranged into a simple funnel. The release warns that differences in local recording affect comparisons; the data do not estimate prevalence nationally or locally.
Changing identification, referrals or recording can change the counts without an equivalent change in underlying abuse. Read them as evidence of service contact and recorded need.
The adult/older-adolescent chapter includes ages 16–17, and WHO includes ages 15–17. Those age bands overlap childhood; never add the adult and childhood headlines together.

title: Methods, sources and downloads
text:
Transformations and checks

WHO: retain age code 15_99, the portal representation of 15 and over, for lifetime non-partner sexual violence. Multiply proportions and interval bounds by 100. Require ordered, non-missing interval bounds within 0–100 and unique country codes. Keep all 138 returned countries, not just chart examples. Preserve underlying-study metadata separately. The API age code is not interpreted as excluding people aged 100+ independently of WHO’s published 15+ definition.
UNODC: retain Violent offences, dimension by type of offence, sex Total, age Total and unit Rate per 100,000 population, for three named sexual-violence categories. Do not mix victim-relationship records, counts or sex-specific records. Assert a unique country/year/category record. Rates are provided by UNODC; this report does not recompute denominators. Rows absent from the source remain absent. E&W, Scotland and Northern Ireland remain separate codes.
ONS trend: parse the downloaded chart CSV, retaining its 16–59 population. Reindex the years so unavailable values appear as gaps, including 2021. Do not interpolate. Do not attach the redesigned 2026 estimate.
Other ONS charts: use downloaded age and childhood chart CSVs. Latest 2026 sex estimates, UNICEF regional figures and Home Office outcome-maturity values are small manually transcribed series from the linked releases, with their exact figures and definitions visible in build_report.py.
UK snapshots: verify the Northern Ireland count against the downloaded PSNI workbook. The England and Wales and Scottish counts are transcribed from their official bulletins. They have different periods and are not aggregated.
Build: verify hashes of retained source downloads before generating charts and tables. Render the complete Quarto site; validate local file links, data uniqueness, labels and chart existence. Raw-source hash validation freezes the edition; adopting revisions requires a reviewed source update.

title: Methods, sources and downloads
text:
Interpretation limits
Denominators: people affected, offences, recorded investigations and service contacts are different units. Percentages of women, all adults and the entire population cannot be freely compared.
Age and time: last-year, since-age-15 and before-age-18 measures answer different questions. Older adolescents overlap the adult-oriented and childhood sources. Retrospective adult reports can omit children currently experiencing abuse and people outside the household sample.
Survey uncertainty: estimates are not exact counts. WHO intervals express model uncertainty. ONS subgroup charts here show point estimates; only source-supported significance statements are made. Disclosure, recall, sample coverage and non-response affect estimates. The absence of a worldwide male adult estimate in this report is an evidence gap, not an assumption that men are unaffected.
Territory: a modelled United Kingdom estimate is not the same statistical geography as an England and Wales survey. Scottish and Northern Irish police series need their own legal and recording context.
Ranks and causes: country ordering does not establish relative safety, policy effects or causes. No inference about individual perpetrators, migration, ethnicity or individual risk follows from these aggregate figures.

title: Methods, sources and downloads
text:
Coverage and access limitations
The WHO and UNICEF PDF downloads were inaccessible in this environment. The report uses WHO’s own portal JSON, definitions and publication page, and UNICEF’s own accessible release. The WHO requested-country list includes seven supported codes without returned estimates; these are not filled. The international portal is accessed as a frozen snapshot, not as a promise of live data.
An additional ONS police-trend CSV request was rate-limited. No chart is constructed from that failed request. The international police comparison instead uses the successfully downloaded UNODC workbook; UK recent counts use the accessible official bulletins. Failed source attempts are recorded in the register.
